421.title: The anthill
421.hook: a riddle of an anthill that smokes by night and blazes by day: the body (MN 23)
421.howItsDone: Theravada teachers sometimes use the anthill riddle to teach the hindrances and the aggregates, and in the Pali discourses naga, a serpent or great elephant, is also an image for an awakened one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the raft, and your line, put the raft down. The teaching is for crossing over, not for carrying on your head.

Late one night in a dark forest, a deity lights up the whole grove and gives a monk named Kumara Kassapa a riddle. There's an anthill, the deity says. It smokes by night and blazes by day. A brahmin said: wise one, take a tool and dig. Digging, the wise one found a bar. Then a bullfrog, a fork in a road, a strainer, a tortoise, a butcher's knife and block, a piece of meat. And at last, a naga, a serpent. And the brahmin said: leave the naga. Don't harm it. Honor the naga. Take this riddle to the Buddha, the deity tells him, and remember his answer.
screen: `A RIDDLE IN THE DARK.` → `IT SMOKES BY NIGHT, BLAZES BY DAY.` → `DIG.`

segments.voice: MN 23, the Vammika. Kumara Kassapa does what he's told, and the Buddha opens the riddle piece by piece. The anthill is this body: made of the four elements, born of mother and father, built up of rice and porridge, subject to wearing away and breaking apart. Smoking by night is lying awake thinking over what you did by day. Blazing by day is acting on those thoughts, in body, speech and mind. The brahmin is the Buddha himself. The wise one is a disciple in training. The tool is noble wisdom. Digging is effort. Then, what the digging turns up. The bar is ignorance. The bullfrog is angry despair. The fork in the road is doubt. The strainer is the five hindrances. The tortoise is the five aggregates, the pieces we take for a self. The knife and block are the five cords of sense pleasure. The piece of meat is delight and lust. Each one: lift it out, throw it away. And the naga is a monk whose taints are destroyed: leave it, honor it. So you dig through layer after layer, the plain, heavy stuff of a mind, and at the bottom you don't find a monster. You find something to honor. The commentary says Kumara Kassapa later reached awakening by working with this very riddle. It was given to a monk still in training, and it took him all the way.
screen: `THE ANTHILL IS THIS BODY.` · `NIGHT THINKING, DAY DOING.` · `BAR, FROG, FORK, STRAINER, TORTOISE.` · `AT THE BOTTOM, A NAGA TO HONOR.` · then, large: `DIG CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Feel the anthill, this body sitting here, built of food and breath, and notice whether it's smoking: thoughts from last night, plans from today, still turning over. Then dig gently, one layer, a fork in the road of doubt or a bullfrog of irritation, and just name what you find, lifting it out on an out-breath.
The anthill. A riddle about the body, dug through layer by layer with wisdom, until there's something at the bottom to honor.
Your line: dig carefully. The tool is wisdom, and the digging is effort. That's day four hundred twenty-one.

422.title: Relay chariots
422.hook: seven chariots in relay, each for one stage of the road
422.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching, the seven purifications from this discourse later shaped Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, where a practitioner's progress is described stage by stage, each purity resting on the one before.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the anthill, and your line, dig carefully. Under layer after layer of obstacles, there was something to honor.

Two monks have heard of each other and never met. One is Sariputta, the Buddha's chief disciple for wisdom. The other is Punna, son of Mantani, praised to the Buddha by the monks of his home country. Sariputta wants to meet him. So he follows Punna into a grove called the Blind Men's Wood, sits down under a tree a little way off, and when the afternoon is ending, walks over and starts asking questions. Punna has no idea who he's talking to.
screen: `TWO MONKS WHO NEVER MET.` → `A GROVE, A TREE, AN AFTERNOON.` → `PUNNA DOESN'T KNOW WHO'S ASKING.`

segments.voice: In the twenty-fourth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, Sariputta asks: why do you live the holy life? For pure virtue? No. For a pure mind? No. For pure view? No. Down a list of seven purities, Punna says no to every one. Then what for? For final release without clinging, Punna says. Then is final release the same as pure virtue? No. Is it something apart from all seven? Also no. So Punna gives a picture. King Pasenadi lives in Savatthi and has urgent business in Saketa, a long way off. He sets out seven chariots in relay along the road. He rides the first to the second, climbs down, rides the second to the third, and so on, until the seventh brings him to the palace gate in Saketa. If someone at the gate asks, did you come here from Savatthi in this chariot, and the king says yes, that's not quite true. The honest answer names the whole relay. Each chariot only had to reach the next one. That's how the seven purities work, Punna says. Pure virtue is for the sake of a pure mind. A pure mind is for the sake of pure view. And so on down the road, until the last purity carries you to release. None of them is the goal. Each is there for the sake of the next. Then the two men learn each other's names, and each praises the other.
screen: `WHY DO YOU LIVE THE HOLY LIFE?` · `SEVEN CHARIOTS FROM SAVATTHI TO SAKETA` · `EACH ONE ONLY REACHES THE NEXT` · `NONE IS THE GOAL; EACH SERVES THE NEXT` · then, large: `ONE STAGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of something long you're in the middle of, a recovery, a degree, a hard year, a habit you're rebuilding, and picture only the next chariot: the one small stretch actually in front of you this week. Then sit with the breath, one breath as one stage, and when the mind runs ahead to the palace gate, bring it back to this chariot.
Relay chariots. Seven purities, each one there to carry you to the next, until the last brings you to release.
Your line: one stage at a time. The road is long; the next chariot is close. Until tomorrow.

423.title: The bait
423.hook: the deer-feeder's crops, laid out to catch four herds
423.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Nivapa Sutta's four herds to describe the middle way between indulgence and harsh denial; monastics and lay meditators practice restraint of the senses and deep concentration as the 'lair' Mara can't reach.

segments.voice: Yesterday: relay chariots, and your line, one stage at a time. Each purity carries you on to the next, until release.
screen: `RELAY CHARIOTS — ONE STAGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: A phone game is free. The first level is easy, the colors are bright, and there's a little gift waiting every morning if you open it. Nobody built that by accident. Somebody sat in a room and planned how you'd be caught, gently, so you'd never feel the net. Twenty-five centuries ago the Buddha described the same room, only with a field and a herd of deer.
screen: `FREE, BRIGHT, A GIFT EVERY MORNING.` → `SOMEBODY PLANNED IT.` → `A FIELD, AND A HERD OF DEER.`

segments.voice: In the twenty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, a deer-feeder plants a crop, not out of kindness, but so deer will come, eat carelessly, and be easy to catch. Four herds come. The first walks straight into the crop, eats without care, grows heedless, and is caught. The second sees this and swears off the crop entirely. They go deep into the forest and live on wild grass, but in the last month of the hot season the grass and water run out. Thin and weak, they wander back, eat wildly, and are caught too. The third herd makes a lair close by and eats carefully, never losing its head. But the deer-feeder notices them, puts up a great fence around the field, finds where they sleep, and catches them as well. The fourth herd makes its lair where the deer-feeder can't go. They eat without losing their heads, and slip away; the feeder and his men can't find them. Then the Buddha explains. The crop is the five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at us. The deer-feeder is Mara, the tempter. The herds are four kinds of seekers: those who dive in, those who run to harsh denial and break, those who stay close and get trapped by opinions, and those who go where Mara can't follow, into deep stillness. Notice the second herd. Running away wasn't enough. Starving wasn't freedom. The way out is neither the crop nor the desert. It's eating without being caught.
screen: `A CROP PLANTED TO CATCH DEER` · `FOUR HERDS: DIVE IN, RUN, HOVER, ESCAPE` · `THE CROP IS THE FIVE CORDS OF PLEASURE` · `RUNNING AWAY WASN'T ENOUGH` · then, large: `THE BAIT IS SET.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time today you reached for something without deciding to, the phone, the fridge, the feed, the cart, and without judging it, see the field it grew in and how bright it looked. Then come back to the breath, which nobody is selling you, and if the pull comes again, watch it rise like a deer lifting its head, and stay where you are.
The bait. The deer-feeder's crop: pleasures laid out on purpose, so we'll eat carelessly and be caught.
Your line: the bait is set. The fourth herd ate, and still slipped away. Day four hundred twenty-three, done.

424.title: The noble search
424.hook: the ignoble search chases what ages; the noble search seeks the unaging
424.carry: worth a search of its own
424.howItsDone: MN 26 is read as the Buddha's own account of his going forth and awakening, and teachers use its two searches to invite reflection on aging, sickness and death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bait, and your line, the bait is set. The herd that got away ate without being caught.

Scroll back through a phone's search history. Shoes. Flights. A better job. Is this mole normal. Houses we can't afford. Whether a certain person is still single. It's a strange and honest diary of what we're hunting for, day after day. In MN 26 the Buddha says there are two kinds of search. And he admits, plainly, which kind he once made himself, before his awakening.
screen: `A SEARCH HISTORY IS A DIARY.` → `WHAT ARE WE HUNTING FOR?` → `TWO KINDS OF SEARCH.`

segments.voice: The Ariyapariyesana Sutta is the twenty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. Ariya means noble; pariyesana means search. In the ignoble search, a person who is themselves subject to aging, sickness and death looks for happiness in things that are also subject to aging, sickness and death. He lists them plainly: wife and children, men and women slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, horses, gold and silver. None of these is wicked. The point is only that they age too: you're chasing something that is running out at the same speed you are. In the noble search, a person who sees that they are subject to aging and death looks for what does not age and does not die: the unborn, the deathless, the supreme security from bondage. Buddhists call it nibbana, nirvana in Sanskrit. Then the Buddha tells his own story, in his own voice. Before awakening, he too was making the ignoble search. Then, while still young, black-haired, in the first stage of life, he shaved his head and went forth, though his mother and father wept. He studied with two teachers, Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, mastered what they taught, and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search. He walked until he reached a pleasant grove at Uruvela with a clear river, sat down, and there found what he was looking for. So the noble search isn't throwing away the shoes or the house. It's noticing what you're asking them to do. They can't stop you aging. Something else might be worth a search of its own.
screen: `ARIYA: NOBLE · PARIYESANA: SEARCH` · `CHASING WHAT AGES, AS YOU AGE` · `SEEKING THE UNAGING, THE DEATHLESS` · `THE BUDDHA'S OWN SEARCH, TOLD BY HIM` · then, large: `THE NOBLE SEARCH.`

segments.voice: Think of the last three things you searched for, on a screen or in your head, and hold each one lightly: will this age? Then ask what in you was looking underneath, rest, safety, to be loved, and let that deeper wish sit with you as you breathe, without solving it.
ariyapariyesana. A being who ages, seeking what does not age.
Your line: worth a search of its own. Nothing wrong with the shoes; they just can't do that job. See you tomorrow.

425.title: The smaller footprint
425.hook: a good tracker doesn't conclude from a small footprint; the gradual training
425.howItsDone: Theravada teachers present MN 27 as a model of the gradual training, from hearing the teaching and keeping precepts to meditation and liberation, and use the tracker's patience to caution students against mistaking early meditative experiences for the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ariyapariyesana, the noble search, and your line, worth a search of its own.

A wanderer named Pilotika is walking back from a visit to the Buddha, full of admiration. The brahmin Janussoni stops him and asks why he's so sure the Buddha is the real thing. Pilotika says: I'm like an elephant tracker who sees a huge footprint and knows, that's a great bull elephant. I've seen four footprints of this man, and I'm sure. The brahmin carries the story to the Buddha. And the Buddha, of all people, says: not so fast.
screen: `PILOTIKA IS SURE.` → `FOUR FOOTPRINTS, ONE GREAT ELEPHANT.` → `THE BUDDHA: NOT SO FAST.`

segments.voice: The shorter discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint, the twenty-seventh of the Middle-Length Sayings, finishes Pilotika's picture properly. A skilled tracker enters an elephant forest and sees a big footprint, long and broad. He doesn't conclude: there are female dwarf elephants with big feet. Then a big footprint, and high marks where the bark is scraped. Still not: tall female elephants could make those. Then tusk marks high on the trees. Still not: tall females with tusks could make those. Only when he sees broken branches too, and then the bull elephant itself, under a tree or in the open, does he say: this is the great one. Then the Buddha lays out the gradual training. Someone hears the teaching, gains trust, and goes forth. They keep the precepts, guard the senses, stay mindful in everything they do, and find a quiet place to sit. The hindrances fall away. They enter the first absorption, then the second, the third, the fourth. Each of these, the Buddha says, is a footprint, and a noble disciple doesn't conclude yet. Then come deep knowledges, and still not. Only at the end, when the mind is freed and they know it's freed, do they say: the teacher is truly awakened, and the teaching is well proclaimed. It's a caution aimed at praise of the teacher himself. A good feeling in meditation is a footprint, not the elephant.
screen: `PILOTIKA'S PRAISE, AND A CORRECTION` · `A BIG PRINT COULD BE A SMALLER ELEPHANT` · `THE GRADUAL TRAINING, STEP BY STEP` · `ONLY THE ELEPHANT ITSELF SETTLES IT` · then, large: `NOT YET THE ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go, and within a few breaths the mind will offer a verdict: this is going well, or this isn't working, or I'm bad at this. Call it a footprint and keep sitting; if another verdict arrives, call that a footprint too, because you're tracking, not deciding.

426.title: The heartwood
426.hook: a man seeking heartwood who settles for twigs, bark or sapwood
426.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the heartwood simile to remind monastics and lay practitioners that reputation, good conduct, concentration and insight are stages of the path, and that liberation of mind is its goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hatthipada, and your line, not yet the elephant. A footprint is a sign worth following, not yet a reason to conclude.

Build a fire with green branches and you meet the problem fast: it smokes, it hisses, it goes out. The good wood is inside, the dense, dark center of an old tree that burns slow and lasts. Carpenters want it too. It doesn't rot, it doesn't warp. But you can't get to it without cutting through everything else first, the leaves, the bark, the pale sapwood, and it's tempting to stop halfway.
screen: `GREEN BRANCHES SMOKE AND GO OUT.` → `THE GOOD WOOD IS AT THE CENTER.` → `TEMPTING TO STOP HALFWAY.`

segments.voice: The twenty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings was given, the text says, not long after Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin, had split away from the community. The Buddha describes a man who needs heartwood. He goes into the forest, finds a great tree, walks past the heartwood, the sapwood, the inner bark and the outer bark, and cuts off twigs and leaves. He carries them home thinking he's got heartwood. A man with good eyes would say: he doesn't know what heartwood is, and his work won't get done. Then the Buddha maps the tree. Someone goes forth out of faith and gains gifts, honor and fame; pleased with that, they look down on others. That's the twigs and leaves. Someone else becomes truly virtuous, but stops, pleased with their virtue: the outer bark. Another reaches deep concentration, and stops there: inner bark. Another reaches knowledge and vision, and stops: sapwood. Then the goal, plainly. This holy life is not for gifts and fame, not for virtue alone, not for concentration alone, not for knowledge and vision alone. It's for the unshakable freedom of mind. That is the heartwood. None of the outer layers is bad. Virtue is good; concentration is good; they're part of the same tree. The mistake is only in stopping, pleased with yourself, and calling bark heartwood.
screen: `TWIGS AND LEAVES: GIFTS AND FAME` · `BARK: VIRTUE, THEN CONCENTRATION` · `SAPWOOD: KNOWLEDGE AND VISION` · `HEARTWOOD: UNSHAKABLE FREEDOM OF MIND` · then, large: `TAKE THE HEARTWOOD.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you care about, your work, your practice, a relationship, and sit with its layers: the twigs and leaves of praise and likes, the bark of good habits around it. Then ask quietly what's at the center, the part that would still matter if nobody saw, and rest your attention there, as if your hand were on the grain of the wood.
The heartwood. Sara in Pali: the dense core of the tree, past the leaves, the bark and the sapwood. The unshakable freedom the path is for.
Your line: take the heartwood. The applause is real, and still not the center. That's day four hundred twenty-six.

original.note: Pali sara: heartwood, the core or essence. the discourse is the Mahasaropama Sutta, the greater simile of the heartwood.

chat.says: If I meditate really well, haven't I got the main thing in Buddhism?
options: In MN 29 concentration is inner bark; the heartwood is unshakable freedom of mind.
Yes. Deep concentration is the heartwood, and the rest is only bark.
No. Meditation is just twigs and leaves, so it's best to skip it.
chat.meaning: MN 29 says the holy life isn't for gifts, virtue, concentration or knowledge alone. It's for the unshakable freedom of mind, the heartwood.

427.title: Milk and water
427.hook: Anuruddha and his friends live blended like milk and water
427.howItsDone: Buddhist monasteries still share chores in much the way MN 31 describes, and the phrase 'like milk and water' is often used by Buddhist teachers to describe the ideal of a harmonious community, lay or monastic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heartwood, and your line, take the heartwood. Today, the end of a week, and three friends in a forest.

Every shared kitchen has the same quiet war. Who finishes the milk and doesn't buy more. Who leaves the pan soaking for three days. Who takes the trash out, every single time, and has started keeping score. Three monks once lived together in a sal-tree wood called Gosinga. When the Buddha came to visit, he asked how they were getting along. Their answer is a recipe.
screen: `THE QUIET WAR IN A SHARED KITCHEN.` → `THREE MONKS IN A SAL-TREE WOOD.` → `HOW ARE YOU GETTING ALONG?`

segments.voice: In the thirty-first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the three are Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila. When the Buddha arrives, the park keeper, not knowing who he is, tries to turn him away so as not to disturb the monks. Anuruddha hears, and comes running. Are you living in harmony? the Buddha asks. Yes, says Anuruddha: we live without quarreling, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. How? I think, how fortunate I am to live with companions like these. I treat them with kindness in deed, word and thought, openly and in private. And I think, why don't I set aside what I want, and do what they want? So I do. We are different in body, he says, but one in mind. Then he describes the kitchen. Whoever comes back first from the alms round sets out the seats and the water. Whoever comes back last eats what's left or throws it out, and puts everything away. Whoever sees the water jar empty fills it. If it's too heavy, he waves a hand for help, and the two of them carry it together, without breaking the silence. And every fifth night they sit up together, talking about the teaching. Milk and water mix so completely you can't pour them apart again. In Anuruddha's telling, that blend is built from small things: a filled jar, a tidied seat, nobody keeping score. And the week looks back: an anthill dug carefully, relay chariots, the bait, ariyapariyesana, a footprint, the heartwood, and now the whole path in a water jar carried by two.
screen: `THE PARK KEEPER TRIES TO TURN HIM AWAY` · `KINDNESS IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT` · `WHOEVER SEES THE JAR EMPTY FILLS IT` · `THIS WEEK: FROM AN ANTHILL TO A JAR` · then, large: `MILK AND WATER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you share space with, a home, an office, a group chat, and try Anuruddha's thought just to see how it feels: how fortunate I am to live with this person. It may feel strange; let it. Then picture one small thing you could do for them without being asked or mentioning it, the jar, the dishes, the trash, and breathe with that picture.
samagga. Lives blended so well they pour as one: kind in deed, word and thought, each setting aside what they want for the others.
Your line: nobody keeping score. Different in body, one in mind, as Anuruddha put it. A week, done.

fork.setup: you're one of the three monks. you come back last from the alms round. there's leftover food and the seats are still out. what do you do?

fork.reveal: in Anuruddha's description, whoever comes back last eats what's left or throws it out, and puts the seats and water away. nobody needs to be asked.

original.note: Pali samagga: in concord, united. after asking after their health and alms, the Buddha asks the three whether they live in concord.

trapdoor: what you thought: harmony means never disagreeing.
what it means: it means kindness in deed, word and thought, and quietly doing your share without keeping score.
what a scholar hears: Anuruddha's formula (kindness of body, speech and mind, openly and in private) reappears in MN 48 among the six qualities that make for harmony.

chat.says: How did those three monks in the forest actually get along so well?
options: Kindness in deed and word, setting aside their own wants, and filling the empty jar.

Anuruddha was in charge, and the other two simply did what he decided.
chat.meaning: In MN 31 Anuruddha says each sets aside what he wants to do what the others want, with kindness in deed, word and thought.
